title: Amortized analysis
lead: An Essential section on amortized analysis: one dynamic array, doubled when full, analysed by the aggregate, accounting and potential methods, then a stack analysed the same three ways; the potential method is Advanced. Here n counts the elements and m the array’s capacity, except in the aggregate analysis, where m is the size of the full array being copied. The stack’s push, pop and multi-pop are defined in its own table; stacks are the subject of Section 3.1.
notes: OI Wiki’s prerequisite line, its list of further reading and its code are not included here; with thanks to the OI Wiki Team and its contributors.
exercise_notes: No open exercise tests this section’s concepts. Its exercises are MIT OpenCourseWare problems with their published solutions, under CC BY-NC-SA, and are kept apart from the book’s CC BY-SA content: 6.046J Fall 2005 problem 6-1 (Electronic Billboard) and 6.046J Spring 2012 problem 6-1 (Amortization in Balanced Binary Trees). 6.046J Spring 2015 problem 4-1 (Extreme FIFO Queues), which needs queues, is held for Section 3.4. The exercises of Erickson’s lecture notes on amortized analysis have no published answers and are left out.

referents.label: n, the number of elements in the array
m, the capacity of the array

footnotes.html: Here m is the size of the full array, the number of elements a resize copies. Later in the section m stands for other things: the capacity of the array, beside n for the number of elements, in the potential method’s example and in its starting value m = 1 above, and the number of operations in the potential method’s principle. Where a resize happens the full array’s size and its capacity are equal, so every count in the section is right in each reading.

derivations.what: the total time cost of m operations and its upper bound
derivations.source: OI Wiki, amortized analysis, the potential method (principle)

then.why: The $i$-th operation takes the data structure from the state $S_{i-1}$ to the state $S_i$.

steps.cap: The sum telescopes: each $\Phi(S_i)$ with $0 < i < m$ is added once and subtracted once, so only $\Phi(S_m) - \Phi(S_0)$ is left.
Since $\Phi(S_m) \geq \Phi(S_0)$, the term $\Phi(S_0) - \Phi(S_m)$ is at most $0$.

derivations.what: the amortized cost of an insert
derivations.source: OI Wiki, amortized analysis, the potential method (example: analysing the resizing of a dynamic array)

assumes.text: An insert that needs no resize adds one element and keeps the capacity: $n$ becomes $n + 1$ and $m$ stays $m$.
An insert that needs no resize writes one element, at actual cost $1$.
The insert that triggers a resize finds the capacity $m = n$; after it there are $n + 1$ elements and the capacity is $2n$.
The insert that triggers a resize copies all $n$ elements into the new array and inserts the new one, at actual cost $n + 1$.
